claims.text: Protective tribochemical oxide layers are the dominant factor governing wear performance of high-entropy-alloy coatings under mechanical sliding.
The proposed test material is an AlCoCrFeNiTi0.5 HEA coating on a steel substrate with a uniform, annealed, and polished initial state.
Changing ambient oxygen partial pressure while holding composition, microstructure, thickness, temperature, and load constant isolates the effect of atmospheric oxygen.
The hypothesis is intended to be tested during elevated-temperature sliding at approximately 400–700 °C.
Ambient oxygen reacts with the HEA wear surface to form an oxide-based tribofilm.
Sliding continually replenishes the oxide tribofilm.
A stable oxide tribofilm protects the coating against direct mechanical contact.
Formation of a protective oxide layer can increase the elevated-temperature wear resistance of AlCoCrFeNiTi0.5.
A protective oxide tribofilm reduces the coefficient of friction.
Increasing oxygen partial pressure produces a more robust tribofilm.
Increasing oxygen partial pressure systematically lowers friction and volumetric wear loss relative to near-vacuum conditions.
Protective oxide formation is minimal or absent in near-vacuum or inert atmospheres for the proposed coating.
Near-vacuum or inert testing produces higher friction and wear than oxidative testing of the same coating.
The proposed mechanism should apply primarily to oxide-forming HEA compositions in moderate-to-high-temperature sliding.
The tribofilm effect may become less pronounced or absent at lower temperatures.
Extremely high loads may suppress or eliminate the protective tribofilm effect.
HEA formulations deficient in oxide-forming elements may not exhibit the protective tribofilm effect.
Minor compositional differences, microstructure, and competing wear mechanisms may alter an HEA system's reliance on tribofilm formation.
